body.text: As stablecoins reshape payments, US banks are turning to blockchain to make deposits faster and more programmable, without abandoning the banking system's existing architecture
Image Source: Getty Images

Thirty-nine United States (US) state banking associations have announced plans for BankChain Alliance, a blockchain network built specifically for the banking sector, targeting a 2027 launch and designed to support stablecoins, tokenised deposits and smart payments. The banking industry will design and operate the network, with interoperability with other networks as a core goal. Kathy Kraninger, interim chair and chief executive officer of the Florida Bankers Association, described the aim as building regulated, secure infrastructure that financial institutions of any size, including small community banks unable to build such a system alone, could use.

The project is seeking a technology partner to lead its development, but its success will depend on regulatory approval and whether member banks route meaningful transaction volumes through a shared network rather than continuing to build proprietary systems.

This initiative should not be read as banks discovering blockchain for its own sake. It is better understood as an institutional response to competitive pressure from stablecoins, which have grown quickly because they let money move as instantly as a message while much of the banking system still settled payments through older infrastructure. The central question BankChain Alliance is trying to answer is whether banks can offer the same instant, programmable experience through deposits—liabilities they already know how to manage and regulate—rather than ceding that function to stablecoin issuers operating outside the banking perimeter.

BankChain Alliance is not an isolated development. It arrives amid a broader, faster-moving wave of bank-led blockchain adoption among the largest US and international institutions. JPMorgan's Kinexys platform, built around its JPM Coin deposit token, has processed more than US$3 trillion in cumulative transactions and now handles billions of dollars in institutional payments daily. It expanded in January 2026 to operate on the Canton Network alongside its original private infrastructure. Citigroup has advanced a parallel effort through Citi Token Services, which it integrated with its round-the-clock dollar clearing system in September 2025 to support multibank cross-border settlement.

BNY has launched a tokenised deposit service for institutional clients, HSBC has introduced a similar offering for corporate customers, and Wells Fargo announced in August 2026 that it would begin offering tokenised deposits to corporate clients that autumn, choosing to join a shared network rather than build a proprietary one. Separately, The Clearing House, backed by banks including JPMorgan, Bank of America, Citi and Wells Fargo, is developing its own bank-owned tokenised deposit network, targeted for launch in the first half of 2027, a schedule nearly identical to that of BankChain Alliance.

Viewed together, these efforts suggest that the state banking associations behind BankChain Alliance are not so much pioneering a new strategy as extending an approach the largest institutions have begun to validate, this time built specifically to give small and mid-sized banks a comparable seat at the table.

The distinction between a stablecoin and a tokenised deposit is more consequential than it first appears. A stablecoin is issued by a crypto-native entity, trades on public blockchains and functions as a bearer instrument, meaning whoever holds it controls it directly, with no issuer relationship in between. In contrast, a tokenised deposit remains a deposit. It sits inside the existing bank regulatory structure, can pay interest and remains a claim on a specific bank rather than an instrument that circulates freely. The trade-off is that tokenised deposits move less easily between banks. BankChain Alliance and similar consortium efforts are trying to address this friction by enabling a deposit token issued by one member institution to be used and recognised across the wider network.

That friction is not incidental; it is part of how the banking system functions. Banks are conventionally described as borrowing short and lending long, accepting deposits that are technically redeemable at any moment while using the same money to fund mortgages and business loans repaid over many years. This arrangement works because deposits behave far more slowly than their contractual terms suggest. Economists capture this using two measures: weighted average life, which shows how long a pool of deposits tends to remain on a bank's books, and deposit beta, which shows how readily that money chases a marginally better interest rate elsewhere.

Research published by Federal Reserve economists Rosie Levy and Srini Ramaswamy in August 2026 found that roughly 80 percent of the interest rate risk banks currently carry—approximately US$ 8.5 of a US$7 trillion total, in 10-year-equivalent terms—is supported by the sluggish, sticky behaviour of ordinary deposits. If tokenisation made deposits move faster and chase yield more aggressively, shrinking their effective duration by just 10 percent, the researchers estimated that banks would lose about US$580 billion of their capacity to fund long-term lending. A 10-percent increase in deposit sensitivity to interest rates would remove a further US$700 billion of that capacity.

The practical consequence of such a shift at scale is not abstract. Banks confronting faster, more rate-sensitive deposits would likely respond by holding larger buffers of highly liquid assets such as Treasuries and central bank reserves to guard against sudden outflows and by relying more heavily on other forms of wholesale borrowing to sustain their loan books, borrowing that tends to be priced closer to what non-bank lenders pay. Both responses point to more expensive and less available credit for households and businesses, as the comparatively cheap, patient funding that deposits currently provide would become scarcer.

Pix is not a precise analogue for tokenised deposits; the direction of the effect—real-time payments pushing banks towards greater liquidity and away from patient credit provision—aligns closely with what Levy and Ramaswamy’s research projects.

Brazil's instant payment system, Pix, offers an early empirical preview of this dynamic. Launched in 2020, Pix reached around 200 million active users by early 2026, processing roughly US$650 billion a month—equivalent to about a quarter of Brazil's annual economic output. A 2025 study using Brazilian regulatory data found that banks whose customers used Pix more heavily held more government bonds and other liquid assets and pulled back on overall credit intermediation. Within the loans they continued to extend, they shifted towards a larger share of subprime lending to compensate for tighter liquidity elsewhere.

Above these institutional and market developments sits a wider debate about what the next-generation monetary system should look like. One framework, proposed by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), holds that any candidate for the backbone of money must satisfy three tests: singleness, meaning it always trades at par with no due diligence required; elasticity, meaning it can expand flexibly to meet the economy's payment needs without gridlock; and integrity, meaning the system resists financial crime.

Under this framework, the BIS judges that tokenised commercial bank deposits fit naturally within the existing two-tier system, with central bank reserves underneath, whereas stablecoins fail all three tests. They are bearer instruments capable of circulating without issuer oversight; they can trade at inconsistent values, undermining singleness; and their structure, which requires fresh cash upfront for any new issuance, constrains elasticity in ways ordinary bank deposits do not.
Banks across the size spectrum now appear to see instant, programmable money as inevitable and are moving to ensure it is built on their own balance sheets rather than around them.

BankChain Alliance sits at the intersection of these developments. It represents an attempt by a broad coalition of banks to offer the speed and programmability that have made stablecoins attractive, without abandoning the underlying architecture of deposits, prudential regulation and deposit insurance that, the BIS argues, keep money trustworthy in the first place. Whether the alliance succeeds will depend on practical questions: selecting a capable technology partner, securing regulatory approval and persuading banks large and small to connect to a shared network rather than build proprietary alternatives, much as JPMorgan, Citi, BNY, HSBC and Wells Fargo have begun to do independently and through The Clearing House.

The broader conclusion, however, extends beyond any single initiative. Banks across the size spectrum now appear to see instant, programmable money as inevitable and are moving to ensure it is built on their own balance sheets rather than around them. If they fail to move quickly enough, the instant-settlement logic that Brazil's Pix has demonstrated at national scale is likely to arrive in the United States through stablecoins instead, on terms banks will have had no part in setting.
